binders: For every natural number m, including m = 0, let V = {0,…,m−1} → ℝ, the real vector space of m coordinates.
For every function q : ℝ → ℝ → V, with spatial argument first and time argument second.
For every function flux : V → V, assigning a flux vector to a state vector.
For every pair of functions qt, fluxx : ℝ → V, serving as specified derivative fields at the selected time.
For every selected time t ∈ ℝ.
The integral-law hypothesis quantifies independently over every a,b,s ∈ ℝ; its time s is not restricted to the selected t.
The other derivative and continuity hypotheses concern the selected t and all real spatial points; the interval hypotheses quantify over every a,b ∈ ℝ.
The conclusion quantifies over every x ∈ ℝ and then existentially over two vectors u,v ∈ V, which may depend on x and all previously fixed data.
hypotheses: For every a,b,s ∈ ℝ, the spatial slice y ↦ q(y,s) is Lebesgue integrable between a and b, and the function τ ↦ ∫_a^b q(y,τ) dy has derivative flux(q(a,s)) − flux(q(b,s)) at τ = s.
For every x ∈ ℝ, the function τ ↦ q(x,τ) has derivative qt(x) at τ = t.
For every x ∈ ℝ, the function ξ ↦ flux(q(ξ,t)) has derivative fluxx(x) at ξ = x.
For every a,b ∈ ℝ, qt is interval integrable from a to b with respect to Lebesgue measure.
For every a,b ∈ ℝ, fluxx is interval integrable from a to b with respect to Lebesgue measure.
For every a,b ∈ ℝ, the function τ ↦ ∫_a^b q(y,τ) dy has derivative ∫_a^b qt(y) dy at τ = t.
The function x ↦ qt(x) + fluxx(x) is continuous on ℝ.
conclusions: For every x ∈ ℝ, there exist u,v ∈ V such that τ ↦ q(x,τ) has derivative u at t, ξ ↦ flux(q(ξ,t)) has derivative v at x, and u + v = 0.

Since the supplied derivative fields identify these derivatives uniquely, the conclusion is equivalently qt(x) + fluxx(x) = 0 for every x, together with the derivative assertions already assumed. In coordinates, ∂_t q_i(x,t) + ∂_x[flux(q(x,t))]_i = 0 for every i ∈ {0,…,m−1}.
mathematical_definitions: V has coordinatewise addition, subtraction, zero, and real scalar multiplication, its finite-product topology, and the standard finite-product norm.
Every derivative is an ordinary two-sided derivative of a real-variable, V-valued function at the stated point.
Interval integrability from a to b means integrability on both (a,b] and (b,a]; equivalently here, integrability between the endpoints regardless of their order.
The oriented interval integral is ∫_a^b f dμ = ∫_(a,b] f dμ − ∫_(b,a] f dμ, where μ is real Lebesgue measure. These are vector-valued Bochner integrals.
The integral balance includes both interval integrability of q at every time and the derivative identity with boundary term flux(q(a,s)) − flux(q(b,s)).
The pointwise differential balance means existence of both relevant derivative vectors and equality of their sum to the zero vector.
translation.proposition_plain_english: For any finite real vector dimension, any state function q defined for all real space and time, any state-to-flux function flux, any selected real time t, and any specified spatial fields qt and fluxx, suppose q satisfies the integral balance on every real interval at every real time: each spatial slice is interval integrable, and the time derivative of its interval integral equals the left boundary flux minus the right boundary flux. Suppose also that at time t the time derivative of q is qt at every spatial point, the spatial derivative of the composed flux is fluxx at every spatial point, both derivative fields are integrable on every finite interval, differentiation of every interval integral at t gives the interval integral of qt, and qt + fluxx is continuous in space. Then at every real spatial point the time derivative of q and the spatial derivative of its composed flux exist and sum to the zero vector.

restrictions_and_vacuity_risks: The dimension is any natural number, with no assumption m > 0. For m = 0, V is a singleton, so all vector identities and derivative assertions are trivial and there are no component equations.
Space and time range over all of ℝ. There is no bounded spatial domain, restricted time interval, or nonnegative-time requirement.

The integral balance is assumed at every real time, whereas the additional derivative, interchange, and residual-continuity hypotheses are imposed only at the selected time t. The conclusion is at that selected time.
The theorem is conditional on the supplied q, flux, qt, and fluxx satisfying all hypotheses; it does not assert existence or uniqueness of a state function satisfying them.
Differentiation under the interval integral is an explicit assumption at t. It is not asserted to follow solely from the pointwise time derivatives.
Continuity is required of the sum qt + fluxx. Separate continuity of qt and fluxx is not explicitly required.

No global continuity or differentiability of flux as a function V → V is assumed. The spatial derivative concerns only ξ ↦ flux(q(ξ,t)); no spatial derivative of q itself or flux Jacobian is specified.
No joint space-time smoothness of q is asserted. Its spatial slices are interval integrable at all times, and its pointwise time derivatives are specified at t.
Integrability is required on every finite interval, not over the entire real line. No decay at infinity is assumed.
Endpoints need not satisfy a < b. Equal endpoints give a zero integral and zero boundary difference, but the hypothesis also covers every nondegenerate interval.
The conclusion holds at every spatial point and in every coordinate, not merely almost everywhere or in a weak or distributional sense.
The conclusion existentially packages derivative vectors separately at each point. It does not introduce additional regularity or a global choice of new derivative fields.
There are no initial conditions, boundary conditions, positivity constraints on the state, entropy conditions, or hyperbolicity assumptions.
